question: What is the average percentage of energy that can be transferred from one trophic level to another trophic level in a food chain?
solution:
The correct answer is __**10**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The average percentage of energy that can be transferred from one trophic level to another in a food chain is approximately **10%**.
 
• This concept is known as the **10% law** of energy transfer, which was put forward by **Raymond Lindeman** in 1942.
 
• According to this law, when energy is passed in an ecosystem from one trophic level to the next, only about 10% of the energy is transferred.
 
• The remaining 90% of energy is lost in various forms such as heat, respiration, and excretion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Trophic Levels:**

 
 
• Trophic levels refer to the different positions that organisms occupy in a food chain.
 
• Primary producers (plants) are at the first trophic level, herbivores at the second, primary carnivores at the third, and so on.
 
• Each level represents a step in the flow of energy and nutrients.
 
 
 
• **Energy Pyramid:**
 
 
• An energy pyramid is a graphical representation of the energy flow in a community.
 
• The pyramid is typically broad at the base and narrows towards the top, indicating the decreasing amount of energy available at each successive trophic level.
 
• This decrease follows the 10% law of energy transfer.
 
 
 
• **Biomass:**
 
 
• Biomass refers to the total mass of living organisms in a given area or ecosystem at a particular time.
 
• It is often used as a measure of energy available at each trophic level.
 
• Like energy, biomass also decreases with each ascending trophic level in a food chain.
 
 
 
• **Ecological Efficiency:**
 
 
• Ecological efficiency is the efficiency with which energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next.
 
• It is typically low, around 10%, meaning that 90% of the energy is lost at each step.
 
• This inefficiency limits the number of trophic levels in an ecosystem.
